options.a: Instrument, sponge, and sharps counts before skin closure
options.b: Correct patient, site/side, and procedure before incision
options.c: Sterilization indicator results for every tray before opening
options.d: Correct patient and procedure after the incision is made

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the time-out with the closing count; counts prevent retained items, while the time-out confirms patient, site, and procedure.
distractorExplanations.c: Indicator checks are part of tray setup by the scrub and circulator, not the Universal Protocol time-out before incision.
distractorExplanations.d: Wrong timing: the time-out is done immediately before the incision, and it must also confirm site/side, not just patient and procedure.

options.a: Head up, feet lowered
options.b: Supine with legs in stirrups
options.c: Seated upright at 45–90°
options.d: Head down, feet elevated

distractorExplanations.a: That is reverse Trendelenburg (head up, feet down), used for upper-abdominal and head/neck cases, not Trendelenburg.
distractorExplanations.b: Supine with legs raised in stirrups is the lithotomy position used for perineal and gynecologic procedures.
distractorExplanations.c: Sitting upright at 45–90° describes Fowler's/semi-Fowler's position, the opposite of the head-down Trendelenburg.

options.a: Proximal to the knees on supine patients
options.b: Directly over the patellae on supine patients
options.c: Across the lower chest of supine patients
options.d: Distal to the knees over the calves

distractorExplanations.b: Placing the strap directly over the kneecaps puts pressure on a bony prominence; the strap goes about 2 inches above the knees.
distractorExplanations.c: A strap across the chest restricts chest expansion and ventilation; the supine safety strap is placed over the thighs above the knees.
distractorExplanations.d: A strap over the calves risks peroneal nerve and venous compression; standard placement is proximal to the knees on the thighs.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-perioperative.explanation: Prevent falls while protecting nerves/skin/ventilation. Place the strap about 2 inches above the knees, secure but not tight enough to cause a tourniquet effect.

options.a: The patient is transferred to the OR table and positioned
options.b: Sterile drapes/packs are opened and arranged with aseptic technique
options.c: The surgical time-out is completed before the skin incision
options.d: The surgeon completes the hand scrub and enters the room gowned

distractorExplanations.a: Transfer and positioning are patient-care steps; the sterile field exists only once sterile packs/drapes are opened aseptically.
distractorExplanations.c: The time-out happens after the field is already set up and the patient draped; it does not create the sterile field.
distractorExplanations.d: The surgeon's scrub and gowning come after the scrub person has opened and arranged the sterile field.

options.a: Reporting a break only when the surgeon or circulator saw it happen
options.b: Correcting breaks quietly without telling the team, to avoid delays
options.c: Honestly acknowledging breaks in sterile technique and correcting them
options.d: Reporting others' breaks in technique to the charge nurse after the case

distractorExplanations.a: Surgical conscience applies whether or not anyone witnessed the break; self-reporting unseen breaks is the core of the concept.
distractorExplanations.b: Silent correction hides the break from the team, who may need to replace items or re-drape; surgical conscience requires speaking up.
distractorExplanations.d: Delayed reporting after the case does not protect this patient; breaks are acknowledged and corrected immediately at the field.

options.a: Wrong-site surgery
options.b: Surgical site infections
options.c: Instrument loss in reprocessing
options.d: Retained surgical items

distractorExplanations.a: Wrong-site surgery is prevented by site marking and the Universal Protocol time-out, not by surgical counts.
distractorExplanations.b: SSIs are reduced by asepsis, skin prep, and prophylactic antibiotics; counts target items left inside the patient.
distractorExplanations.c: Instrument tracking in sterile processing is an inventory issue; OR counts exist to prevent items being retained in the patient.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-perioperative.explanation: Initial, additional item, closure, and final counts per policy; document discrepancies. Counts cover sponges, sharps, and instruments.

options.a: Certain anesthetics/succinylcholine
options.b: Local anesthetics such as lidocaine
options.c: Nondepolarizing agents such as rocuronium
options.d: Nitrous oxide and IV opioids

distractorExplanations.b: Amide local anesthetics like lidocaine are an outdated myth as MH triggers; they are considered safe in MH-susceptible patients.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses depolarizing with nondepolarizing relaxants: succinylcholine triggers MH, rocuronium/vecuronium do not.
distractorExplanations.d: Nitrous oxide and opioids are non-triggering agents used in MH-safe anesthetics; volatile gases and succinylcholine are the triggers.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-perioperative.explanation: MH crisis needs dantrolene and team response; scrub may help with sterile needs/cooling support per role. Triggers are volatile anesthetic gases and succinylcholine; the CST should know the MH cart and team roles.

options.a: Begin the initial count aloud so it is finished before the incision is made
options.b: Maintain a calm environment and be ready to assist with airway emergencies
options.c: Start the skin prep so the incision can begin once intubated
options.d: Turn the patient to the surgical position as induction drugs are given

distractorExplanations.a: Counting aloud during induction adds noise and distraction; the room should be quiet so anesthesia can manage the airway.
distractorExplanations.c: Prep and draping wait until the airway is secured and anesthesia approves positioning; starting early distracts and risks the patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Positioning is done after induction and airway control with anesthesia's approval, not while induction drugs are being given.

options.a: Verify the drug name with the circulator and label the container after the case ends
options.b: Verify drug name, strength, and expiration with the circulator and label the container
options.c: Accept the drug when the vial is shown, then label containers once every med is on the field
options.d: Verify drug name and dose against the surgeon's preference card, labeling syringes only

distractorExplanations.a: Labels must be applied immediately when the drug is received; labeling after the case leaves unlabeled meds on the field.
distractorExplanations.c: Seeing the vial is not verification, and batch labeling later is unsafe; each drug is read back and labeled as it is received.
distractorExplanations.d: The preference card lists what the surgeon prefers, not the drug in hand; every container (cups, basins, syringes) must be labeled.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-perioperative.explanation: Medication safety requires read-back verification and immediate labeling. Label every container on the field immediately.

options.a: Neckline to waist in front and back, with sleeves to the shoulder
options.b: Chest to sterile field level / gloved hands to elbows anteriorly
options.c: Chest to the hem in front, with sleeves from shoulder to cuff
options.d: Shoulders to waist anteriorly, including the axillary area

distractorExplanations.a: The back of the gown is never in view and is considered unsterile; the neckline and shoulders are also excluded.
distractorExplanations.c: The gown below sterile field (table) level is unsterile, and the shoulders/axillae are excluded from the sterile sleeve area.
distractorExplanations.d: Shoulders and axillae are friction areas that are considered unsterile; the sterile front starts at the chest.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-asepsis-steri.explanation: Backs, below waist, and axillae are not considered sterile. The back of the gown is not considered sterile.

options.a: The field stays sterile because the saline is sterile, so no action is needed
options.b: The wet area becomes safe again once it dries, so let it air-dry before use
options.c: The wet area is contaminated by strike-through risk and must be handled per protocol
options.d: The surgeon decides at closure whether the wet spot needs further attention

distractorExplanations.a: Sterile fluid still wicks through the drape and carries organisms from below (strike-through); the fluid's sterility does not protect the field.
distractorExplanations.b: Drying does not reverse contamination; once strike-through has occurred, the area stays contaminated until covered or replaced.
distractorExplanations.d: Contamination is managed immediately by the scrub team (cover or replace), not deferred to the surgeon at closure.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-asepsis-steri.explanation: Wicking through drapes contaminates; manage wet spots appropriately. Typical handling is to cover the wet area with an impervious drape or replace the item.

options.a: Peel the pack and let the item slide across the unsterile edges
options.b: Tear the pack through the center and present it to the scrub
options.c: Peel the pack toward the body and lean over the field to present
options.d: Peel edges back without touching contents, presenting to scrub

distractorExplanations.a: The outer edges of a peel pack are unsterile; letting the item slide across them contaminates it.
distractorExplanations.b: Tearing through the middle contaminates the contents; peel packs are opened by rolling the edges back along the seal.
distractorExplanations.c: Peel packs are opened away from the body, and the circulator must not reach or lean over the sterile field.

options.a: Assisted gloving
options.b: Open gloving
options.c: Closed gloving
options.d: Indicator double-gloving

distractorExplanations.b: Open gloving is self-gloving with hands out of the cuffs (e.g., re-gloving or catheter insertion), with no team member assisting.
distractorExplanations.c: Closed gloving is self-gloving with the hands kept inside the gown cuffs; no other person holds the glove.
distractorExplanations.d: Indicator double-gloving describes wearing two pairs to reveal punctures, not who helps put the gloves on.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-asepsis-steri.explanation: Know open, closed, and assisted gloving; double-gloving reduces puncture risk. Closed gloving is done with hands inside the gown cuffs; open gloving is done with hands outside.

options.a: Used whenever a tray is short, as long as a chemical indicator is included
options.b: Avoided when possible; if used, follow IFU and aseptic delivery for immediate use
options.c: Performed on the dropped item without cleaning, since the cycle sterilizes it
options.d: Used, then the item stored on the shelf for later cases if the indicator passes

distractorExplanations.a: IUSS is not a fix for inventory shortages; it is reserved for urgent need when no packaged replacement exists.
distractorExplanations.c: Sterilization fails on soiled items; a dropped instrument must be cleaned before any sterilization cycle.
distractorExplanations.d: IUSS items are for immediate use only and must not be stored for later cases, even if indicators pass.

options.a: Hands only to the wrists using the timed method before gloving
options.b: Hands and forearms after gowning, before closed gloving
options.c: Hands and forearms for the timed/counted method per product IFU
options.d: The patient's skin at the incision site before draping

distractorExplanations.a: The surgical scrub covers the hands and forearms to about 2 inches above the elbows, not just to the wrists.
distractorExplanations.b: Wrong sequence: the surgical scrub is done before entering the OR and gowning, not after the gown is on.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the surgical hand scrub with the patient skin prep done by the circulator or scrub before draping.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-asepsis-steri.explanation: Waterless surgical hand rubs also used per IFU after washing when indicated. The scrub is done before gowning.

options.a: A fixed expiration date printed on the package label passes
options.b: The external chemical indicator tape changes color
options.c: Thirty days pass on the shelf for wrapped trays
options.d: Compromised by tears, moisture, or improper handling/storage

distractorExplanations.a: That describes time-related sterility; event-related sterility depends on what happens to the package, not a printed date.
distractorExplanations.b: The indicator tape changes color during processing to show exposure to the sterilant; it does not mark loss of sterility.
distractorExplanations.c: A fixed 30-day shelf life is a time-related policy; event-related sterility has no set day count.

options.a: Positive pressure, HEPA filtration, and minimizing traffic/talking over field
options.b: Negative pressure, HEPA filtration, and keeping doors open for airflow
options.c: Positive pressure, with doors propped open to increase air exchanges
options.d: Low air exchange rates and humidity under 10% to limit microbial growth on surfaces

distractorExplanations.b: Negative pressure is for decontamination and airborne isolation rooms; ORs are positive pressure with doors kept closed.
distractorExplanations.c: Open doors disrupt positive pressure and let corridor air in; OR doors stay closed to maintain air exchanges.
distractorExplanations.d: ORs need high air exchange rates (about 20 per hour) and humidity of roughly 20–60%, not low exchanges and very dry air.

options.a: Pull a new glove over the punctured one and continue the case
options.b: Step away from the field and re-glove using sterile technique
options.c: Finish the current step, then re-glove at the next count
options.d: Rinse the glove with sterile saline and continue if no blood is seen

distractorExplanations.a: Layering a new glove over a punctured one leaves the contaminated glove in place; the punctured glove must be removed and replaced.
distractorExplanations.c: A punctured glove is contaminated immediately; delaying the change to the next count exposes the patient and the scrub.
distractorExplanations.d: Rinsing does not restore a breached barrier, and absence of visible blood does not mean the glove is intact.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-asepsis-steri.explanation: Immediate correction protects patient and self; double-glove helps detect punctures. Change the gown too if indicated.

options.a: A nonsterile item touches it or sterility is broken by moisture strike-through
options.b: The circulator walks around the field while facing it at a safe distance
options.c: The lights are adjusted by the circulator without touching the field
options.d: Sterile team members pass each other back-to-back at a distance during the case

distractorExplanations.b: Facing the field while keeping a safe distance is the correct way for nonsterile staff to move around it; it does not contaminate.
distractorExplanations.d: Passing back-to-back (or front-to-front) is the accepted technique for sterile team members and keeps the field sterile.
distractorExplanations.c: Not the best answer here; the right answer is “A nonsterile item touches it or sterility is broken by moisture strike-through”.

options.a: In front from neckline to hem and sleeves from shoulder to cuffs
options.b: In front from chest to sterile field level and sleeves to cuffs
options.c: In front and back from chest to waist, with sleeves to the elbow
options.d: In front from chest to sterile field level, excluding the sleeves

distractorExplanations.a: The neckline, the area below field level, and the shoulders are not considered sterile on a gown.
distractorExplanations.c: The back is never considered sterile, and the sleeves are sterile down to the cuffs, not just to the elbow.
distractorExplanations.d: The sleeves (from about 2 inches above the elbow to the cuff) are part of the sterile gown area.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-asepsis-steri.explanation: Standard sterile gown areas are limited; backs and below-waist are unsterile. Sterile practice standards define these limits.

options.a: Pass front-to-back, facing the other's back
options.b: Pass front-to-front or back-to-back
options.c: Pass back-to-front with hands at the sides
options.d: Pass side-to-side with arms folded at the axillae

distractorExplanations.a: Front-to-back puts one sterile front against an unsterile back; only front-to-front or back-to-back is acceptable.
distractorExplanations.c: Back-to-front still pairs a sterile front with an unsterile back, and hands at the sides drop below the sterile zone.
distractorExplanations.d: Side-to-side brings sterile fronts near unsterile backs, and the axillae are unsterile, so arms are not folded there.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-asepsis-steri.explanation: Passing technique protects gown fronts and the sterile field. Keep distance from nonsterile areas while passing.

options.a: The drape's adhesive strip has failed and needs re-taping
options.b: Moisture has penetrated, potentially contaminating the field
options.c: Electrosurgical current has passed through the drape material
options.d: A sharp instrument has punctured the drape without any fluid

distractorExplanations.a: Adhesive failure is a draping problem but not strike-through, which specifically means fluid soaking through the material.
distractorExplanations.c: Strike-through refers to moisture penetration, not electrical current; it is unrelated to electrosurgery.
distractorExplanations.d: A dry puncture is a separate breach; strike-through is defined by moisture wicking through the drape.

options.a: Sliding the item over the peeled edges and onto the back table drape
options.b: Presenting the item so the sterile person can take it without contaminating edges
options.c: Having the scrub reach into the pack and pull the item past the edges
options.d: Peeling the pack back toward the body while reaching over the sterile field

distractorExplanations.a: The peeled edges are unsterile; sliding the item over them contaminates it before it reaches the field.
distractorExplanations.c: Pulling the item past the edges lets it brush unsterile surfaces; the item is presented so it lifts cleanly out.
distractorExplanations.d: Peel packs are opened away from the body, and the circulator must never reach over the sterile field.

options.a: Right upper quadrant
options.b: Left upper quadrant
options.c: Right lower quadrant
options.d: Epigastric region

distractorExplanations.b: The left upper quadrant holds the spleen and stomach body; the gallbladder lies on the right under the liver.
distractorExplanations.c: The right lower quadrant holds the appendix and cecum, not the gallbladder.
distractorExplanations.d: The epigastric region contains the stomach and pancreas; the gallbladder sits in the RUQ on the liver's undersurface.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-anatomy-surg-.explanation: Cholecystectomy addresses RUQ anatomy; know triangle of Calot concepts at high level. It lies on the undersurface of the liver.

options.a: Separation of the wound edges after primary closure of the incision
options.b: Abnormal passage connecting two epithelial surfaces
options.c: Protrusion of tissue/organ through a defect in the cavity wall
options.d: Collection of pus walled off within the abdominal wall

distractorExplanations.a: That describes wound dehiscence; a hernia is tissue protruding through a defect in the cavity wall.
distractorExplanations.b: An abnormal passage between two epithelialized surfaces is a fistula, not a hernia.
distractorExplanations.d: A walled-off pus collection is an abscess; hernias involve protrusion of tissue or organ through a wall defect.

options.a: Jejunum
options.b: Stomach
options.c: Gallbladder
options.d: Duodenum

distractorExplanations.a: The jejunum follows the duodenum; the common bile duct empties at the ampulla of Vater in the second part of the duodenum.
distractorExplanations.b: Bile does not enter the stomach normally; the CBD drains into the duodenum distal to the pylorus.
distractorExplanations.c: The gallbladder stores bile via the cystic duct; the common bile duct carries bile away from it to the duodenum.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-anatomy-surg-.explanation: CBDE/ERCP anatomy relevant to biliary surgery complications. Drainage is via the ampulla of Vater.

options.a: Posterior to the trachea in the neck
options.b: Anterior to the trachea in the neck
options.c: Lateral to the carotid sheath in the neck
options.d: Anterior to the larynx above the hyoid

distractorExplanations.a: The esophagus lies posterior to the trachea; the thyroid wraps the anterior and lateral trachea.
distractorExplanations.c: The carotid sheath lies lateral to the thyroid lobes, so the gland is medial to it, not lateral.
distractorExplanations.d: The thyroid sits below the larynx at about the 2nd–4th tracheal rings, not above the hyoid bone.

options.a: Clean (no entry into respiratory, GI, or GU tracts)
options.b: Clean-contaminated (controlled entry into GI or GU tract)
options.c: Contaminated (major break in sterile technique/spillage)
options.d: Dirty-infected (old traumatic wound or existing pus)

distractorExplanations.a: That defines Class I (clean); Class III involves spillage, a major break in technique, or a fresh traumatic wound.
distractorExplanations.b: Controlled entry into a hollow tract without spillage is Class II (clean-contaminated), not Class III.
distractorExplanations.d: Old traumatic wounds and existing infection define Class IV (dirty-infected), one class above Class III.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-anatomy-surg-.explanation: Classification guides antibiotic expectations and SSI risk counseling. Class III also includes open, fresh accidental wounds.

options.a: Retractors, drains, antibiotic irrigation, and wound closure strips
options.b: Heparinized saline, vasodilators, and topical antibiotic powder
options.c: Sponge counts, mesh placement, and prophylactic antibiotics
options.d: Clamps, ligatures, electrosurgery, clips, and topical agents

distractorExplanations.a: Retractors expose the field and drains remove fluid; none of these items stop bleeding from vessels.
distractorExplanations.b: Heparinized saline and vasodilators promote flow rather than control bleeding; antibiotic powder targets infection.
distractorExplanations.c: Counts prevent retained items, mesh repairs defects, and antibiotics prevent SSI; none achieve hemostasis.

options.a: Ileocolic artery trunk
options.b: Appendiceal artery
options.c: Right colic artery
options.d: Inferior mesenteric artery

distractorExplanations.a: The appendiceal artery branches from the ileocolic artery; ligating the ileocolic trunk would devascularize the cecum and ileum.
distractorExplanations.c: The right colic artery supplies the ascending colon and is not within the mesoappendix.
distractorExplanations.d: The IMA supplies the left colon and rectum; the appendix is a midgut structure supplied via the SMA branches.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-anatomy-surg-.explanation: The appendiceal artery supplies the appendix via the mesoappendix. It runs within the mesoappendix.

options.a: On the superior/posterior aspect of the testis
options.b: On the anterior surface of the testis
options.c: Within the spermatic cord above the testis
options.d: Posterior to the bladder base, near the prostate

distractorExplanations.b: The epididymis lies on the posterior (and superior) aspect of the testis; the anterior surface is covered by tunica vaginalis.
distractorExplanations.c: The structure running in the spermatic cord is the vas deferens, which continues from the epididymis.
distractorExplanations.d: Posterior to the bladder base near the prostate are the seminal vesicles, not the epididymis.

options.a: Spinal accessory nerve
options.b: Recurrent laryngeal nerve
options.c: Hypoglossal nerve
options.d: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

distractorExplanations.a: The spinal accessory nerve is at risk in posterior triangle (neck dissection) surgery, not near the inferior thyroid artery.
distractorExplanations.c: The hypoglossal nerve runs above the hyoid near the submandibular region, far from the inferior thyroid artery.
distractorExplanations.d: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery, not the inferior thyroid artery.

options.a: A double layer of peritoneum hanging from the stomach
options.b: A peritoneal fold connecting the liver to the lesser curvature
options.c: A fan-shaped fold attaching the small bowel to the posterior wall
options.d: The serous membrane lining the inner abdominal wall

distractorExplanations.b: The fold from the liver to the lesser curvature is the lesser omentum, not the greater omentum.
distractorExplanations.c: The fan-shaped fold suspending the small bowel is the mesentery proper.
distractorExplanations.d: The lining of the abdominal wall is the parietal peritoneum, not the omentum.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-anatomy-surg-.explanation: Greater omentum is a peritoneal apron from the greater curvature of the stomach. It can wall off infection.

options.a: An active electrode and a dispersive (return) pad with good contact
options.b: An active electrode with two tines and no separate return pad
options.c: An active electrode and a return pad placed over a bony prominence
options.d: An active electrode and a return pad over the nearest metal implant

distractorExplanations.b: Two tines and no return pad describes bipolar electrosurgery; monopolar needs a dispersive pad.
distractorExplanations.c: Bony prominences give poor contact and concentrate current, risking pad-site burns; use well-vascularized muscle.
distractorExplanations.d: Metal implants can concentrate current; the pad is placed away from implants on well-vascularized tissue.

options.a: Through the patient to a dispersive pad
options.b: Between the two tines of the forceps
options.c: From the active tip to the grounded table
options.d: Along a vibrating ultrasonic blade

distractorExplanations.a: Current through the patient to a dispersive pad is the monopolar circuit, not bipolar.
distractorExplanations.c: Current to a grounded table is an alternate-site burn hazard with older grounded systems, not the bipolar path.
distractorExplanations.d: A vibrating blade describes ultrasonic (harmonic) devices, which use mechanical energy, not bipolar current.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-equipment-saf.explanation: Bipolar useful near nerves/wet fields with localized current. No dispersive pad is required.

options.a: Any tinted safety glasses, a door sign, and shiny instruments to aim the beam
options.b: Wavelength-specific eyewear and dry towels around the site to absorb the beam
options.c: Eyewear specific to wavelength, controlled access, and nonreflective precautions
options.d: Prescription glasses as eye protection and the laser kept in ready mode between uses

distractorExplanations.a: Eyewear must match the laser's wavelength and OD; shiny instruments reflect the beam instead of being nonreflective.
distractorExplanations.b: Dry towels can ignite; wet towels/sponges are placed around the site to absorb stray laser energy.
distractorExplanations.d: Prescription glasses do not filter laser wavelengths, and the laser goes to standby between uses.

options.a: Hypothermia from loss of limb blood flow
options.b: Fluid overload when the cuff is deflated
options.c: Sterile field contamination from cuff leaks
options.d: Nerve injury, ischemia, and tissue damage

distractorExplanations.a: Tourniquet time limits protect nerves and muscle; hypothermia is not the classic over-time complication.
distractorExplanations.b: Deflation causes reperfusion and possible hypotension, not fluid overload; excess pressure/time causes nerve and tissue injury.
distractorExplanations.c: The cuff sits outside the field; overinflation and excess time injure nerves and tissue rather than contaminating the field.

options.a: Used for the current case, then reported at the end of the day
options.b: Reported and removed from service until repaired
options.c: Repaired on the spot by the scrub tech using spare parts
options.d: Tagged with a note but kept in use until biomed arrives

distractorExplanations.a: Using known faulty equipment risks crush or fall injuries; it must be removed from service before use, not reported later.
distractorExplanations.c: Repairs are done by biomedical engineering, not by the scrub tech improvising during the case.
distractorExplanations.d: Tagging alone is not enough; a defective table is taken out of service until biomed repairs and clears it.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-equipment-saf.explanation: Equipment failure can cause crush/fall/positioning injuries. Do not keep using it carefully.

options.a: Filtered by a standard surgical mask worn by the team
options.b: Cleared by the room's general HVAC air exchanges
options.c: Evacuated with appropriate smoke evacuation systems
options.d: Vented out by opening the OR doors during activation

distractorExplanations.a: Standard surgical masks do not filter the fine particles in plume; local smoke evacuation is required.
distractorExplanations.b: General room ventilation does not capture plume at the source; a smoke evacuator near the tip is needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Opening OR doors disrupts positive pressure and spreads plume to corridors; doors stay closed and plume is evacuated.

options.a: Bipolar electrosurgery
options.b: Harmonic ultrasonic shears
options.c: Pulse oximetry probes
options.d: Monopolar electrosurgery

distractorExplanations.a: Bipolar is the preferred safer option with implanted devices because current stays between the tines.
distractorExplanations.b: Ultrasonic shears use mechanical vibration, not electrical current, so they do not interfere with pacemakers.
distractorExplanations.c: Pulse oximetry uses light sensing and does not interfere with pacemakers or ICDs.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-equipment-saf.explanation: Use bipolar when possible, short bursts, pad placement strategies per protocol. Coordinate monopolar use with anesthesia/cardiology protocols.

options.a: Neutral zone/no-hands passing techniques and proper sharps containers
options.b: Hand-to-hand passing of scalpels with the blade pointed down
options.c: Two-handed recapping of hypodermic needles before returning them to the field
options.d: Leaving loaded needle holders on the Mayo stand with points up

distractorExplanations.b: Hand-to-hand passing of sharps is what neutral-zone technique replaces, regardless of blade direction.
distractorExplanations.c: Two-handed recapping is a major needlestick cause; use one-handed scoop or a recapping device if needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Exposed needle points left upright cause sticks; needles are secured or placed in a needle counter.

options.a: Recount once, and if still off, document the discrepancy and close the wound
options.b: Notify surgeon, recount, search wound/field/trash, and obtain imaging if unresolved
options.c: Search the floor and trash first, then tell the surgeon after the final count is done
options.d: Obtain imaging right away and skip the recount since the film is definitive

distractorExplanations.a: Documenting and closing without searching or imaging leaves a possible retained item; an unresolved count requires imaging.
distractorExplanations.c: The surgeon is notified immediately so the wound can be explored before closure, not after the final count.
distractorExplanations.d: The recount and search come first; imaging is used when the count stays unresolved and can miss some items.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-equipment-saf.explanation: Never falsify counts; retained items are never events. Follow facility policy for the search.

options.a: Applied over a bony prominence close to the operative site
options.b: Applied to clean, dry, well-vascularized skin with full contact per IFU
options.c: Applied to clean, dry skin over the metal hip implant nearest the incision
options.d: Applied to hairy skin after wetting with alcohol for better contact

distractorExplanations.a: Bony prominences have poor contact and concentrate current, risking burns; place the pad over well-vascularized muscle.
distractorExplanations.c: Metal implants can concentrate current; the dispersive pad goes away from implants on well-vascularized tissue.
distractorExplanations.d: Hair reduces contact, and alcohol is flammable and should never pool under a pad; clip hair and keep skin dry.

options.a: Recount at the end of closure and note the discrepancy on the count sheet
options.b: Notify the surgeon, search systematically, and use imaging
options.c: Complete closure, then obtain an X-ray in PACU if the sponge is still missing
options.d: Report the discrepancy only in an incident report after the patient leaves

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting until closure ends removes the chance to search the wound; the surgeon is notified immediately.
distractorExplanations.c: Imaging is done before the patient leaves the OR when a count is unresolved, not after closure in PACU.
distractorExplanations.d: An incident report may follow, but the discrepancy must be resolved with the surgeon and team during the case.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-equipment-saf.explanation: Count discrepancies require immediate communication and resolution steps. Imaging is used as directed by protocol.

options.a: High-frequency alternating current passing through the tissue
options.b: High-frequency mechanical vibration that denatures protein
options.c: Focused light energy absorbed by tissue water
options.d: Extreme cold delivered through a probe to freeze tissue

distractorExplanations.a: Alternating current through tissue is electrosurgery; harmonic devices use mechanical vibration instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Focused light energy absorbed by tissue describes a laser, not ultrasonic shears.
distractorExplanations.d: Freezing tissue with a probe is cryosurgery; ultrasonic shears generate heat from vibration and friction.

options.a: Inflate to the highest cuff pressure available and report time at closure
options.b: Document tourniquet time and follow safe pressure/time limits
options.c: Place the cuff over the bony joint nearest the incision site
options.d: Deflate and reinflate the cuff every 10 minutes to restore flow

distractorExplanations.a: Pressure is set to the lowest effective level per limb and patient, and time is tracked and announced during the case.
distractorExplanations.c: The cuff goes on the proximal limb over muscle, not over a joint or close to the incision.
distractorExplanations.d: Reperfusion intervals are in hours (about 2 hours for a leg per policy), not every 10 minutes.

options.a: Filtered with standard surgical masks
options.b: Evacuated with appropriate smoke evacuation
options.c: Cleared by routine OR air exchanges
options.d: Suctioned through the fluid suction line without a filter

distractorExplanations.a: Standard surgical masks do not filter the small particles in plume; source evacuation is required.
distractorExplanations.c: General OR ventilation does not capture plume at the source, so staff still inhale it.
distractorExplanations.d: An unfiltered fluid suction line can be damaged and does not remove plume safely; use a filtered evacuator.

nbstsa-cst-readiness-check-equipment-saf.explanation: Surgical smoke contains hazardous particulates; evacuation protects the team. This reduces inhalation exposure.
